Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$$
and
$$\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}_C=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

If $C,D$ are coalgebras, a **coalgebra map** $f:C\to D$ is a $k$-linear map satisfying
$$
\Delta_D\circ f=(f\otimes f)\circ\Delta_C,\qquad \varepsilon_D\circ f=\varepsilon_C.
$$
The equations say exactly that $f$ preserves comultiplication and counit.

The defining equations are properties; they do not assert existence for every vector space.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let $f:V\to V'$ be an injective linear map and let $W$ be a $k$-vector space. Then $f\otimes\mathrm{id}_W:V\otimes W\to V'\otimes W$ is injective. Moreover, if $U\subseteq V$ and $Z\subseteq W$ are subspaces and $p:V\to V/U$, $q:W\to W/Z$ are the quotient maps, then, viewing $U\otimes W$ and $V\otimes Z$ as subspaces of $V\otimes W$ through the injections of the first part and the inclusions $U\subseteq V$, $Z\subseteq W$,
$$\ker(p\otimes q)=U\otimes W+V\otimes Z .$$

Let $f:M\to M'$ be a homomorphism of right $R$-modules and $g:N\to N'$ a homomorphism of left $R$-modules. There is a unique group homomorphism

$$f\otimes g:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow M'\otimes_RN'$$

such that $(f\otimes g)(m\otimes n)=f(m)\otimes g(n)$. These maps satisfy

$$\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_N=\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes_RN}$$

and

$$(f'\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ g)=(f'\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes g).$$

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. A subset $N\subseteq M$ is a **submodule** when
it is a subgroup of the additive group of $M$ and is closed under scalars:

$$r\in R,\ n\in N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad rn\in N.$$

The operations on $N$ are the restrictions of those of $M$. Write $N\le M$ when
the ring and module are understood.

Let $N\le M$ be a submodule of a left $R$-module. Since the additive group of
$M$ is abelian, $N$ is normal, so the additive quotient group $M/N$ consists of
the cosets $m+N$. Its proposed scalar action is

$$r(m+N):=rm+N.$$

The well-definedness and module laws are established in
[[thm-quotient-module-laws]]. The resulting module is the **quotient module**
$M/N$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For the regular object take $\rho_C=\Delta$. The coalgebra coassociativity identity is exactly $(\rho_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_C=(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\rho_C$, and its two counit identities give $(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_C=\operatorname{id}_C$ (and the other counit identity), so $(C,\Delta)$ is a right comodule by the coalgebra definition [F2].

Let $M$ have ordered basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$. By [F8], the coordinate functions $\lambda_i:M\to k$ are linear. For each $j$, write $\rho_M(v_j)=\sum_s x_s\otimes d_s$ as a finite tensor by [F3], expand each $x_s=\sum_i\lambda_i(x_s)v_i$, and collect $c_{ij}:=\sum_s\lambda_i(x_s)d_s$. Applying $\lambda_r\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ recovers $c_{rj}$, so the expansion $\rho_M(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\otimes c_{ij}$ is unique.

Let $K=\ker f$, $I=\operatorname{im}f$, and let $q:M\to M/K$ be the quotient. The map $\bar f:M/K\to N$, $\bar f(m+K)=f(m)$, is well-defined and injective: equal cosets have difference in $K$, and $\bar f(m+K)=0$ implies $m\in K$. Thus $f=\bar f q$, so functoriality [F5] gives $f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C=(\bar f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)(q\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)$. By [A1] and [F4], $\bar f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ is injective, while the kernel formula in [F4] with $U=K$ and $Z=0$ gives $\ker(q\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes C)$. Therefore $\ker(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes C\to M\otimes C)$. The same tensor-injection result makes the inclusion $K\otimes C\to M\otimes C$ injective.

Apply coassociativity to $v_j$ and use the expansion in 1.2 to get $\sum_{i,\ell}v_i\otimes c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_{ij})$. Applying $\lambda_r\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ gives $\Delta(c_{rj})=\sum_\ell c_{r\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}$. Applying $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon$ to $\rho_M(v_j)=v_j$ and then applying $\lambda_r$ gives $\varepsilon(c_{rj})=\delta_{rj}$.

For $x\in K$, the comodule-map equation gives $(f\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(x)=\rho_N(f(x))=0$. By 2.1, $\rho_M(x)$ has a unique preimage in $K\otimes C$ under the injective map $i\otimes\operatorname{id}$, where $i:K\hookrightarrow M$; define $\rho_K(x)$ to be that preimage. This is linear because it is the inverse of a linear isomorphism onto its image. The identity $(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_K=\rho_Mi$ and the injectivity of $i\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id}$ show that coassociativity of $\rho_K$ follows from coassociativity of $\rho_M$; injectivity of $i$ and the same identity show its counit law. Hence $K$ is a subcomodule and $i$ is a comodule map.

Conversely, suppose the displayed matrix identities hold. Define $\rho(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\otimes c_{ij}$ on the basis and extend by the unique coordinates in [F8]. For each basis vector, $(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_j)=\sum_{i,\ell}v_i\otimes c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_{ij})=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(v_j)$ by the coproduct identity; also $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\delta_{ij}=v_j$. The maps in each identity are linear and the basis spans $M$, so both identities hold on every vector; hence this is a right comodule.

Factor $f$ as $M\xrightarrow{q_I}I\xrightarrow{j}N$, where $q_I$ is onto and $j$ is inclusion. Define $\rho_I(q_I(m)):=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)$. If $q_I(m)=q_I(m')$, then $m-m'\in K$; by 2.2, $\rho_M(m-m')$ lies in the image of $K\otimes C$, which $q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}$ kills, so the formula is well-defined. It is linear and satisfies $\rho_Iq_I=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M$. Precomposing the coassociativity identity for $\rho_I$ with the surjection $q_I$ gives $(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$, so it holds by coassociativity on $M$ and surjectivity of $q_I$. Likewise, precomposing its counit identity with $q_I$ gives $q_I(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=q_I$, which holds by counitality on $M$; surjectivity gives the identity on $I$. Thus $\rho_I$ is a coaction. Since $f=j q_I$ is a comodule map, $\rho_Nj q_I=(f\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_I q_I$; surjectivity of $q_I$ proves $\rho_Nj=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_I$, so $j$ is a comodule map.

Let $i:J_0\to M$ be an injective comodule map and set $J=i(J_0)$. By step 3.2, $J$ has the image coaction making its inclusion a comodule map. Let $\pi:M\to M/J$ be the quotient and set $\bar\rho(m+J):=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)$. If $m$ is replaced by $m+j$, the difference is $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(j)=0$ because $\rho_M(j)$ is the image of a tensor in $J\otimes C$; hence $\bar\rho$ is well-defined. It is linear and $\bar\rho\pi=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M$. Precomposing its coassociativity identity with the surjection $\pi$ gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$, so it holds by coassociativity on $M$ and surjectivity of $\pi$. Precomposing its counit identity with $\pi$ gives $\pi(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\pi$, which follows by counitality on $M$; surjectivity gives the identity on $M/J$. Thus the quotient is a comodule and $\pi$ is a comodule map.

The map $\widetilde f:M/K\to I$, $m+K\mapsto f(m)$, is the same induced map as $\bar f$ with codomain restricted to $I$. It is injective by the definition of $K$ and onto by the definition of $I$, hence is a vector-space isomorphism. The quotient and image coaction formulas in steps 3.2 and 4.1 give $\rho_I\widetilde f=(\widetilde f\otimes\operatorname{id})\bar\rho$. Since $\widetilde f$ and its tensor map are isomorphisms, composing this identity with their inverses shows $\widetilde f^{-1}$ is also a comodule map.

Step 1.1 establishes the regular comodule; steps 1.2, 2.1, and 3.1 prove both directions of the finite coefficient-matrix characterization. Steps 1.3, 2.2, 3.2, 4.1, and 5.1 establish the kernel, image, quotient, and first-isomorphism claims under AC.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, let $W=\{0\}$ with its zero coaction; both coaction equations are zero equalities, so it is a finite-dimensional subcomodule containing $m$. Otherwise write $\rho(m)=\sum_{s=1}^r x_s\otimes d_s$ as a finite tensor by [F2]. Let $D=\operatorname{span}\{d_1,\dots,d_r\}$; choose a finite basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$ of $D$, express each $d_s$ in that basis, and collect terms to obtain $\rho(m)=\sum_{i=1}^q v_i\otimes c_i$ with the $c_i$ linearly independent. Set $W=\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_q\}$, a finite-dimensional subspace by [F5].

Coassociativity applied to this expansion gives $\sum_i\rho(v_i)\otimes c_i=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_i)$. Let $\pi:M\to M/W$ be the quotient and apply $\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$; the right side is zero since every $v_i\in W$, so $\sum_i ((\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho(v_i))\otimes c_i=0$ in $((M/W)\otimes C)\otimes C$.

Apply the associator and symmetry to rewrite the last equality as $\sum_i c_i\otimes((\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i))=0$. The $c_i$ are independent, so [F3] gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i)=0$ for every $i$. By [F4], each $\rho(v_i)$ lies in the image of $W\otimes C\to M\otimes C$. Therefore $\rho(W)$ lies in that image.

Now suppose $C$ is finite-dimensional, without assuming AC. The construction in step 1.1 still gives $W$ and independent $c_i$. Coassociativity and the quotient map give the zero tensor equality of step 2.1. The finite-dimensional clause of [F3] therefore gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i)=0$ for each $i$.

The inclusion $i:W\hookrightarrow M$ tensored with $C$ is injective by [A1] and [F4]. Hence each $\rho(w)$ for $w\in W$ has a unique lift $\rho_W(w)\in W\otimes C$; uniqueness makes $w\mapsto\rho_W(w)$ linear and $(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=\rho i$. The map $i\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ is also injective. Applying it to $(\rho_W\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W$ gives $(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho i$; applying it to $(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes\Delta)\rho_W$ gives $(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho i$. These are equal by coassociativity of $M$, so injectivity proves coassociativity on $W$. Also $i(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho i=i$; injectivity of $i$ proves counitality. Thus $(W,\rho_W)$ is a finite-dimensional subcomodule. Finally $m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\sum_i v_i\varepsilon(c_i)\in W$ by [F1].

Choose a finite basis $d_1,\dots,d_t$ of $C$ and write $\rho(v_i)=\sum_s y_s\otimes d_s$. Applying $\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}$ and then the coordinate functional dual to $d_s$ gives $\pi(y_s)=0$, hence each $y_s\in W$; so $\rho(v_i)$ is in the image of $W\otimes C$. The inclusion $W\otimes C\to M\otimes C$ is injective without AC here: if $\sum_s w_s\otimes d_s$ maps to zero, applying $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes d_s^*$ gives $w_s=0$ for each $s$. Thus the coaction lifts uniquely and linearly to $W$. The same argument with the finite basis $d_s\otimes d_t$ makes $W\otimes C\otimes C\to M\otimes C\otimes C$ injective. Applying this inclusion to the two coaction composites on $W$ gives the corresponding composites on $M$, which agree by coassociativity; hence coassociativity holds on $W$. Likewise, applying $W\hookrightarrow M$ to its counit composite gives the identity on $W$ by counitality on $M$, and injectivity gives counitality on $W$. Finally, step 2.1 and counitality directly give $m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\sum_i v_i\varepsilon(c_i)\in W$.

Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 prove the arbitrary-$C$ case under AC; steps 2.1, 3.2, and 5.1 prove the finite-dimensional-$C$ case without AC. In both cases the exhibited $W$ is finite-dimensional and is a subcomodule containing $m$.

Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$$
and
$$\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}_C=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

If $C,D$ are coalgebras, a **coalgebra map** $f:C\to D$ is a $k$-linear map satisfying
$$
\Delta_D\circ f=(f\otimes f)\circ\Delta_C,\qquad \varepsilon_D\circ f=\varepsilon_C.
$$
The equations say exactly that $f$ preserves comultiplication and counit.

The defining equations are properties; they do not assert existence for every vector space.

Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

For a coalgebra $C$ over $k$, write
$$
C^*:=\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,k)
$$
for its full algebraic dual, using [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. Define the **convolution candidate product** by
$$
(f*g)(c):=(f\otimes g)(\Delta(c))
$$
for $f,g\in C^*$ and $c\in C$, and take $\varepsilon$ as its candidate unit. Thus, when $\Delta(c)=\sum_i c_i\otimes d_i$, $(f*g)(c)=\sum_i f(c_i)g(d_i)$. Every such sum is finite because tensors are algebraic tensors under [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]].

The theorem [[thm-hh-comodules-and-rational-dual-modules]] proves that this product is associative and unital, so it makes $C^*$ a $k$-algebra. A **left $C^*$-module** here is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-bilinear action $C^*\times M\to M$ satisfying $f\cdot(g\cdot m)=(f*g)\cdot m$ and $\varepsilon\cdot m=m$. This is the usual unital module convention of [[def-left-and-right-modules]] for the resulting $k$-algebra.

Such a module is **rational** if for every $m\in M$ there exists a finite tensor $t_m\in M\otimes C$ such that
$$
f\cdot m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f)(t_m)
\quad\text{for every }f\in C^*.
$$
This definition asserts existence only. The theorem proves uniqueness of $t_m$ under its stated choice hypothesis before naming it as a coaction value.

The convolution formula uses the order $f$ on the first tensor factor and $g$ on the second. Sources that identify $(C\otimes C)^*$ with $C^*\otimes C^*$ using the reversed tensor-factor convention require the corresponding switch; the formula above fixes the convention used throughout this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $v_1,\dots,v_n\in V$ be linearly independent vectors in a $k$-vector space $V$ and let $w_1,\dots,w_n\in W$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\otimes w_i=0$ in $V\otimes W$. Then $w_i=0$ for every $i$; equivalently, the linear map $W^n\to V\otimes W$, $(w_i)\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes w_i$, is injective.

If $V$ is finite-dimensional the same conclusion is proved without the Axiom of Choice.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $f,g,h\in C^*$ and $c\in C$, bilinearity of the pairing defines $f*g\in C^*$. The two values $((f*g)*h)(c)$ and $(f*(g*h))(c)$ are evaluations of $f\otimes g\otimes h$ on $(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta(c)$ and $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(c)$, respectively; these tensors agree by [F1], so convolution is associative. The two counit equations in [F1] give $(\varepsilon*f)(c)=f(c)=(f*\varepsilon)(c)$ for every $c$, so $\varepsilon$ is a two-sided unit. Thus the candidate product in [F3] is a unital associative algebra product.

Given a right comodule $(M,\rho)$, the map $C^*\times M\to M$, $(f,m)\mapsto(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)$, is bilinear. Writing $\rho(m)=\sum m_0\otimes m_1$, coassociativity gives
 $f\cdot(g\cdot m)=\sum m_0 f(m_{1,1})g(m_{1,2})=\sum m_0(f*g)(m_1)=(f*g)\cdot m$.
The counit equation gives $\varepsilon\cdot m=\sum m_0\varepsilon(m_1)=m$. Hence this is a left $C^*$-module.

For every $m$, the existing tensor $\rho(m)\in M\otimes C$ represents the entire orbit because $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)=f\cdot m$ for every $f$. This proves rationality without AC. If $t,t'\in M\otimes C$ both represent that orbit, then $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)(t-t')=0$ for all $f\in C^*$, where $C^*$ is the full algebraic dual [F7]; [A1] and [F4] imply $t=t'$.

Now let $M$ be a rational left $C^*$-module. For each $m$ choose its representing tensor $t_m$ from [F3]; by [A1] and [F4] it is unique. Define $\rho(m):=t_m$. For $m,n$ and $a\in k$, the tensors $\rho(m+n)$ and $\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ have the same evaluation under every $f\in C^*$ because the action is bilinear; the same holds for $\rho(am)$ and $a\rho(m)$. Separation [F4] gives $\rho(m+n)=\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ and $\rho(am)=a\rho(m)$, so $\rho$ is linear.

Suppose now $C$ is finite-dimensional, without using AC. Let $c_1,\dots,c_n$ be a finite ordered basis with dual basis $c_1^*,\dots,c_n^*$ by [F8]. For any left $C^*$-module vector $m$, put $t_m=\sum_{i=1}^n(c_i^*\cdot m)\otimes c_i$. For $f=\sum_i f(c_i)c_i^*$, one has $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)t_m=\sum_i f(c_i)(c_i^*\cdot m)=f\cdot m$, so every module vector is rational. The representing tensor is unique because the dual basis coordinates recover its first-factor coefficients. This finite-coordinate argument uses no basis extension or arbitrary choice.
Evaluation at the unit functional $\varepsilon$ gives $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\varepsilon\cdot m=m$ by the module unit law. Thus $\rho$ is counital.

Fix $m$ and write $\rho(m)=\sum_i m_i\otimes c_i$. Set $T=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(m)-(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)\in M\otimes C\otimes C$. For any $f,g\in C^*$, evaluation of the first term by $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f\otimes g$ is $\sum_i g(c_i)(f\cdot m_i)=f\cdot(g\cdot m)$, while evaluation of the second term is $\sum_i(f*g)(c_i)m_i=(f*g)\cdot m$. The module associativity law makes these equal. Hence every such pairing annihilates $T$. For fixed $g$, the tensor $(\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes C}\otimes g)(T)\in M\otimes C$ is annihilated by every $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f$, so it is zero by [A1] and [F4]. Since this holds for every $g$, a second application of [F4] to the last $C$ factor gives $T=0$. Thus $\rho$ is coassociative.

If $u:M\to N$ is a comodule map, then $f\cdot u(m)=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)\rho_N(u(m))=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)=u(f\cdot m)$ for every $f,m$, so $u$ is a module map. Conversely, if $u$ is a module map, then $(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(\rho_N(u(m))-(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m))=f\cdot u(m)-u(f\cdot m)=0$ for every $f$. The difference is a finite tensor in $N\otimes C$, so [A1] and [F4] make it zero. Hence $u$ is a comodule map.

In the finite-dimensional case, every finite tensor in $X\otimes C$ has a unique expansion $\sum_i x_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluating against each $c_i^*$ recovers $x_i$. Every finite tensor in $X\otimes C\otimes C$ likewise has an expansion $\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\otimes c_i\otimes c_j$, and evaluations against $c_i^*\otimes c_j^*$ recover all coefficients. Therefore the separation uses in steps 1.3, 1.4, 2.2, and 2.3 can all be carried out without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional. Together with step 1.5, this proves the full object and morphism correspondence in that branch without AC.

Steps 1.1–1.3 construct a rational module from every right comodule and recover its unique original coaction; steps 1.4, 2.1, and 2.2 construct a right coaction from every rational module; step 2.3 proves the correspondence on maps. Steps 1.5 and 3.1 prove the full correspondence without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over a field $k$. The regular pair $(C,\Delta)$ is a right $C$-comodule. If $f:M\to N$ is a right-comodule map, then $\ker f$ and $\operatorname{im}f$ inherit right-comodule structures, the quotient $M/\ker f$ is a right comodule, and the induced map $M/\ker f\to\operatorname{im}f$ is a comodule isomorphism, assuming AC. For a finite-dimensional right comodule $M$ with ordered basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$, write
$$
\rho(v_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\otimes c_{ij}.
$$
Then
$$
\Delta(c_{ij})=\sum_{\ell=1}^n c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j},
\qquad
\varepsilon(c_{ij})=\delta_{ij}.
$$
Conversely, any $n^2$ elements $c_{ij}\in C$ satisfying these two identities define a right-comodule structure on the vector space with basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ by the displayed formula.

For a field $k$ and an integer $n\geq1$, let $E_n$ be the vector space with basis $c_{ij}$ for $1\leq i,j\leq n$. The linear maps defined on this basis by
$$\Delta(c_{ij})=\sum_{\ell=1}^n c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j},\qquad \varepsilon(c_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$$
make $E_n$ a coalgebra. In particular, the one-dimensional space with basis $c$ and maps $\Delta(c)=c\otimes c$, $\varepsilon(c)=1$ is a nonzero coalgebra.
